partial.type_support: rosidl_typesupport_c/cpp dispatched to matching introspection C/C++; a 5/5 bidirectional rclcpp/rclpy Docker/netem matrix routes 64-element nav_msgs/Path messages, nested PoseStamped/header/time fields, PoseStamped control messages, SetBool, and nav_msgs/GetPlan through the UDP router with zero invalid frames. GetPlan validates nested start/goal/tolerance requests and a 512-pose response in both language directions; its 73181-byte serialized response exceeds the 65507-byte UDP datagram limit and therefore proves service-frame fragmentation/reassembly. A separate generated FleetShape service passes 5/5 and 10/10 language directions at every declared bound: string<=32, uint8[16], float32[<=128], PoseStamped[<=16], Duration, uint32[<=64], and bounded response string. Dynamic serialization/take loads an optional rosidl_dynamic_typesupport plugin at runtime. rmw_get_publishers_info_by_topic/rmw_get_subscriptions_info_by_topic now report a real RIHS type hash (via the type support handle's own get_type_hash_func) for this process's own local endpoints instead of the zero-initialized/unset sentinel, verified against std_msgs/String (docker_topic_type_hash_probe); this is local-endpoint hash reporting only, not RMW_MIDDLEWARE_SUPPORTS_TYPE_DISCOVERY (deferred type support population for a remotely-discovered, not-yet-known type over the wire), which remains unclaimed. Non-introspection typed publish/take, additional common service families, and full middleware type discovery remain unsupported
partial.qos: KEEP_LAST, lifespan, deadline metadata, reliability transport subset, ROS 2-compatible profile checking across reliability, durability, deadline, liveliness kind, and liveliness lease duration with ERROR/WARNING reason aggregation, and rmw_dds_common-backed BEST_AVAILABLE endpoint adaptation at create time. The 5/5 BEST_AVAILABLE artifact covers publisher/subscription discovery selection, zero-endpoint defaults, mixed-publisher liveliness/max-lease selection, actual-QoS reporting, and frozen policy after churn
partial.reliability: source-sequence ACK/NACK repair and unrecoverable-loss notices carry subscriber identity; only reliable readers emit ACK/NACK and participate in rmw_publisher_wait_for_all_acked snapshots, while best-effort readers detect sequence gaps without requesting repair. Cumulative ACKs use an immutable reception-baseline floor: after first observing sequence 4, later reordered observations 1,5,2 cannot cumulatively acknowledge unseen sequence 3, while each observed frame is still exactly ACKed. A deterministic frame regression covers that 4,1,5,2 order, and the repaired 32-robot/seed-29 Docker/netem row delivers 320/320; an explicitly resumed same-hop artifact then reaches 36/36 while preserving the other 35 rows. A separate deterministic Docker regression drops sequence 2 and repairs it by NACK, then drops sequence 1 and repairs it by timeout retransmission; both phases receive all payloads. If a requested reliable sample has already left writer history, the writer emits a targeted loss notice and the reader advances without NACKing forever; repair admission/budget/attempt exhaustion uses the same terminal path. The three policy-terminal paths each pass 5/5 two-container Docker/netem runs with clean teardown. rmw_publisher_wait_for_all_acked waits for every still-matched reliable endpoint and honors zero, finite, and infinite timeout behavior. Its v2 local 5/5 contract proves that writes published after a wait begins do not extend that wait, two concurrent waiters on one publisher both complete, a reader unmatch releases its pending obligation, BEST_EFFORT returns immediately, and foreign/null handles fail closed. In addition, a four-container UDP/router/netem gate repeats 5/5: a deliberately delayed second remote ACK yields RMW_RET_TIMEOUT at 1/2 ACKs and OK at 2/2, with one DATA and both ACKs observed and forwarded by the router. Cross-language service discovery now schedules a middleware-default bounded five-retry/100 ms repair window on a background worker, so rmw_send_request returns after the initial send and no runner override is required. A matching response cancels pending repair by client endpoint and sequence; client destruction clears it. Pending repair jobs have global/per-client admission bounds; a 5/5 gate reaches exact limits 4/3 while preserving all initial sends. Request/response queues, pending-response state, dedupe history, and response replay are bounded and covered by 5/5 resource/isolation gates. Optional strict-priority, smooth weighted round-robin, and EDF service schedulers each have separate 5/5 Docker/netem evidence with aging/starvation bounds. Opt-in completed-response replay writes a bounded mode-0600 ledger through temporary-file fsync, atomic rename, and directory fsync; a 5/5 SIGKILL gate proves replacement-process replay without duplicate application delivery. This covers completed responses across process crash, not the ambiguity window before persistence, application-side transactional effects, host power-loss durability, or DDS wire interoperability. The reliable retransmission ledger already bounds each publisher's retained history using qos.depth for KEEP_LAST (a fixed 4096-entry cap otherwise), a narrow, repair-purpose equivalent to DDS resource_limits rather than the full policy. This RMW's earlier claim that ROS 2 messages carry no DDS key/instance notion was factually wrong: rosidl_typesupport_introspection_c/cpp's MessageMember::is_key_ genuinely tracks the OMG IDL4 @key annotation -- it is simply unreachable from the legacy .msg grammar, which has no annotation syntax at all, so only a hand-authored .idl can set it, and in practice no shipped ROS 2 message package uses one. The retransmit ledger now uses that field: when a message type declares one or more top-level scalar @key fields, each publisher's history bound applies per DDS-style instance (one @key value combination) rather than to the whole publisher, while a message with no @key field keeps the exact prior per-publisher-only bound, byte-for-byte, since every currently shipped message type falls in that case. A dedicated KeyedInstanceSample.idl fixture and a 5/5 fleetrmw_keyed_instance_retransmit_probe gate prove both halves: 10 samples interleaved across 2 instances at depth=3 retain 6 entries total (3 per instance, independently), while the same interleave on a keyless message type retains exactly 3 total, unchanged. This remains narrow: there is still no max_instances bound (a publisher emitting unboundedly many distinct @key values grows the ledger without limit across instances even though each instance is individually capped), no reader-side per-instance bound, and no support for a @key field that is an array or nested inside a sub-message. Full DDS writer-history/resource-limit semantics and full exactly-once semantics remain unclaimed
partial.fragment_assembly_retention: Idle partial-assembly retention is configurable from 1000 to 600000 ms and defaults to 60000 ms, aligned with bounded writer fragment history. Exact expiration and discarded-missing-index counters are exported. A raw-UDP Docker gate observes four admitted partial assemblies before a configured 1000-ms TTL and then requires exactly four expirations/four discarded missing indexes. The matched 16-robot/32-KiB/seed-7 rerun previously reached only 111/160 with zero expiration, eviction, queue failure, or queue rejection, falsifying premature assembly expiry as the frontier bottleneck. That rerun's dominant limiter has since been root-caused separately (an uncaught ENOBUFS send failure crashing the publisher, see loss_resilient_large_sample_fragment_repair); with it fixed, the identical scenario now reaches 157/160 with TTL expirations still exactly zero, confirming assembly expiry remains cleared as a cause while fleet-scale reliability remains correctly unclaimed short of 160/160
partial.initial_fragment_round_robin: Initial large-sample fragments use per-frame round-robin queues and an adaptive initial-versus-repair scheduler whose burst falls from 8 to 4, 2, or 1 under repair pressure. A deterministic 8-frame Docker gate reaches contention, limits same-frame service to one while contended, emits authenticated completion markers, delivers 8/8 with complete ACK, and exits 0/0/0. Trailing repair opens after the last fragment, a validated completion marker, or a no-progress guard measured only from newly received fragments. A raw-UDP gate streams 20 duplicates for 1.53 seconds and observes the exact trailing 2-3 NACK at 436 ms under a 400-ms guard; all 20 duplicates are counted without refreshing progress. The 16-robot/32-KiB/seed-7 MTU-budgeted row had improved from 152/160 to 155/160 but left four publisher topics unacknowledged. After separately root-causing that scenario's dominant limiter (an uncaught ENOBUFS send failure crashing the publisher, see loss_resilient_large_sample_fragment_repair), the identical row now reaches 157/160 with 3 assemblies still hitting NACK exhaustion, so fleet-scale reliability remains correctly false short of 160/160
partial.udp_datagram_budget: FLEETQOX_RMW_UDP_DATAGRAM_BUDGET_BYTES computes each effective fragment chunk from the requested size, fragment metadata, AES-GCM envelope, and configured X.509/signature overhead; oversized wire payloads enter repair-capable fragmentation before protection and every final datagram is checked fail-closed. The runner defaults to the IPv4/UDP MTU-1500 payload budget of 1472 bytes while the C++ default remains disabled for compatibility. A deterministic gate requests 4096-byte chunks, obtains 1409-byte effective chunks and exact 1472-byte wire high-water on both hops, records eight reductions, zero budget/send failures, 8/8 delivery, complete ACK, and 0/0/0 teardown. The latest lossy 16-robot row reaches 155/160 after duplicate fragments stop refreshing progress, versus 152/160 before that fix and 154/160 in the prior 1024-byte row. This remains negative frontier evidence. Automatic IPv4 path-MTU discovery is now implemented and probed: the socket enables kernel PMTU discovery mode, reads back the discovered MTU via a connected probe socket on synchronous EMSGSIZE and via the IP_RECVERR error queue on asynchronous ICMP fragmentation-needed notices, and, instead of rejecting an oversized send with an opaque kernel failure, retries it once through the existing loss-resilient fragmentation path at the learned budget so a single too-large publish is delivered rather than fatal to the caller (see docker_udp_pmtu_discovery_probe). It only ever shrinks the learned budget and never re-probes if a path later improves; IPv6/header variation (this transport is IPv4-only), secure credential amortization, that PMTU-recovery gap, and multi-seed completion remain open
partial.loss_resilient_large_sample_fragment_rep: Opt-in plaintext-frame fragmentation assigns a stable frame identity before per-chunk AEAD/signing. Protected frames that exceed the UDP payload ceiling are also forced onto this per-fragment protected path instead of the legacy pre-authentication outer wrapper. Receivers accumulate 1024-byte chunks, wait for assembly quiescence, request observed internal holes before guarded trailing indexes, retain bounded completed-frame tombstones to reject late whole-frame duplicates, encode bounded missing-index ranges, and send fragment NACKs to the exact UDP source. The per-NACK index cap is configurable and automatically reduced under fleet pressure so eligible assemblies share a hard 512-index repair sweep budget. A deterministic 513-assembly Docker gate lowers the first 512 requests from 8 to 1 index, caps that sweep at exactly 512, then serves the final assembly with the configured eight-index cap from the rotating cursor on the next sweep; exact cumulative-index, reduction, maximum-sweep, and exhaustion telemetry is required. Active partial assemblies have configurable count and total-size admission bounds; metadata collisions are dropped without erasing an existing assembly. A raw-UDP Docker gate injects six partial assemblies against limit four plus one oversize fragment and one metadata collision, then requires active=4, missing=4, evictions=2, oversize drops=1, mismatch drops=1, and clean exit. A second two-peer ROS 2 Docker gate sends six distinct AES-256-GCM-protected fragmented samples with one deliberately omitted chunk each; strict AEAD admission retains exactly four assemblies/four holes, evicts exactly two, decrypts protected traffic without authentication failure, delivers zero incomplete samples, and rejects unprotected repair and outer fragment wrappers before either can consume a reassembly slot. A three-peer Docker campaign independently recreates credentials, network, and processes five times; each run establishes this state through an allowed SROS2 X.509 identity, then has a CA-trusted attacker with the same PSK sign and encrypt six large fragmented samples. All 5/5 runs preserve active assemblies, missing indexes, evictions, decrypted-frame count, and last verified identity while denying 481 attacker data/graph inputs in total, at least 95 per run. This proves repeated bounded unauthorized-identity pressure isolation, not a long-duration or multi-attacker production soak. Senders retain bounded history and retransmit only requested chunks through separate bounded initial/repair queues with initial-traffic fairness, duplicate pending and recent-repair coalescing, configurable admission backpressure, global pacing, and queue/failure/high-water/deferral counters. Fragment NACK receipt marks a reliable ledger frame as observed so timeout retransmission does not compete with its selective repair; never-observed frames retain a separately paced whole-sample fallback. Active assembly, missing-index, age, NACK/history exhaustion, suppression, fallback-deferral, requested-index, and fleet-budget-reduction metrics make the scale boundary auditable. The generic serialized relay spends its bounded reliability horizon in wait_for_all_acked before teardown. A fail-closed Docker probe deliberately drops fragment index 2 from each of two exact 32768-byte messages, disables whole-sample timeout retransmission, then requires exactly two selective retransmissions, 2/2 relay delivery, complete ACK, zero queue failure/rejection, and clean 0/0/0 process teardown. A current roaming-loss scale-0.25 run delivers 40/40 through both hops with clean 0/0/0 process teardown and complete relay downstream ACK; one upstream publisher ACK remains pending in that stochastic run. That negative 16-robot/seed-7 figure has since been root-caused, not just re-measured: the publisher's UDP sendto() intermittently hit ENOBUFS (kernel send-buffer exhaustion) under this link's combined fragment volume, and every occurrence was fatal -- one failed send raised an uncaught rclpy RCLError that crashed the whole publisher process instead of being retried, discarding every sample still queued behind it. A separate, unrelated harness bug also made the standard repro command for this exact scenario (run_ros2_relay_rmw_netem_probe.py --robot-count 16 ...) fail before ever reaching the network: write_relay_probe_scripts never substituted the __STATE_PAYLOAD_BYTES__ placeholder its own imported publisher template requires, so any 16-robot rerun crashed with a NameError at publisher startup. With the transient-error retry added and the harness bug fixed, three fresh seed-7/13/29 reruns deliver 153-157/160 (95.6-98.1%) with zero publisher crashes -- a large improvement, but still short of 160/160, so fleet-scale reliability remains correctly unclaimed. The default FLEETQOX_RMW_FRAGMENT_NACK_MAX_REQUESTS=6 and FLEETQOX_RMW_FRAGMENT_TAIL_GUARD_MS=1000 turn out to be conservative for this same 33.6x-oversubscribed load (see benchmark_offered_load_sensitivity): raising them to 40 and 2000 ms respectively (env override, C++ default unchanged pending a cross-test compatibility check) lifts a 10-run sample at the identical load from 0/10 fully-passing runs to 4/10 exactly-160/160 runs, with the relay-forwarded hop alone reaching 160/160 in 7/10. The residual failures are two independent, genuinely stochastic lossy hops (publisher-to-relay and relay-to-subscriber) racing a fixed test timeout under 33.6x oversubscription -- deterministic 100% is not a realistic target at this specific offered load without adaptive capacity control (unclaimed below); the tuning does meaningfully raise the odds of full delivery on any given run and is worth carrying as the effective operating configuration for fleets expecting sustained loss under contention. Adaptive capacity control, sustained multi-identity credential-rotation pressure, arbitrary sample sizes, repeated fleet-scale/resource-pressure evidence, and production reliability remain unclaimed
partial.wait_sets: subscriptions, services, clients, domain-scoped automatically triggered graph guard conditions for local/remote add/remove/descriptor/QoS changes and remote lease expiry, max_conditions enforcement with zero meaning unbounded, null-entry rejection, active/same-context validation, and exact entity-owner node validation. Unread status readiness is implemented for every non-invalid Jazzy rmw_event_type_t: offered/requested deadline missed, liveliness lost/changed, offered/requested incompatible QoS, message lost, publisher/subscription incompatible type, and publication/subscription matched. A 5/5 Docker matrix executes seven production probes per round (35/35 components), checks initial/cleared not-ready controls, and consumes ready statuses through rmw_take_event. Separate event-family DDS semantics and remote production boundaries remain scoped
partial.transport: UDP reference transport/router plus POSIX SHM local path and de-duplicated SHM-local/UDP-remote hybrid; UDP large-frame fragmentation/reassembly is implemented for RMW endpoints with router fragment passthrough. The legacy ngtcp2/GnuTLS H3 gateway probes remain available as a subprocess fallback, including async enqueue/drain, session/tp/token file plumbing, repeated local/netem soak, publish POST, and take GET evidence. An optional in-process ngtcp2 0.12.1/GnuTLS 3.8.3/nghttp3 0.8.0 H3 client is integrated into both rmw_publish and on-demand rmw_take_serialized_message: the Docker/netem proof executes 128 publishes plus one take over one QUIC v1 connection, one verified TLS handshake, 129 bidirectional streams, 128 same-connection reuses, zero reconnects, three client-native qlogs plus three server qlogs, and an untrusted-CA fail-closed control. Its final independent rmw_publish and rmw_take calls run from two threads and rendezvous into concurrent POST/GET streams before either response is driven; an explicit paired transport API provides a second positive control. The pairing window is opt-in and unmatched calls fall back to normal single-stream execution. A stateful aioquic QUIC v1/H3 FleetQoX gateway now validates real FleetRMW data frames, keeps bounded per-domain/topic history, deduplicates publisher sequence numbers, and maintains independent consumer replay cursors; a 5/5 Docker/netem proof exercises exact replay through verified TLS, persistent client sessions, qlogs, and fail-closed HTTP status propagation. A separate 5/5 six-container netem gate loads a client certificate/key into the in-process GnuTLS client and requires mutual TLS at the gateway: one trusted client is admitted while missing-certificate and unrelated-CA clients are rejected before state mutation. An additional certificate signed by the trusted CA but carrying a mismatched SPIFFE-style publisher URI SAN receives HTTP/3 403 because opt-in identity binding requires the URI suffix to equal the FleetRMW publisher_id; it also cannot mutate gateway state. A current, correctly signed client CRL is validated at startup and a CA-trusted certificate whose serial is listed is rejected during TLS authentication. The client CRL is now also reloaded fresh from disk for every new connection rather than only once at service startup, so a serial revoked while the gateway is already running is rejected on the very next connection with no restart, verified by a probe that revokes a previously accepted certificate live against a running gateway (docker_quic_gateway_live_crl_reload_probe); a reload failure fails closed by never authenticating that connection rather than falling back to stale revocation state. The aioquic 0.9 compatibility path uses a guarded private TLS hook, so native upstream client-auth support, broader fleet identity policy, certificate rotation, accepted 0-RTT/resumption, clustered durability, congestion/admission integration, and production readiness remain unclaimed
partial.public_ngtcp2_gateway: The pinned official ngtcp2/GnuTLS server uses public APIs for mTLS and exports initialized smoothed RTT, RTT variation, congestion window, bytes in flight, PTO count, and raw per-stream packet-loss count over backend protocol v2. Only RTT and RTT variation enter opt-in admission scoring; raw loss count remains separate because no sent-packet denominator is exposed. The matched 5/5 Docker/netem contrast changes the same frame from HTTP 429 to accepted/taken HTTP 200 with source ngtcp2_public_api and zero external observation requests. Stateful Unix-socket dispatch is offloaded from libev to a configurable bounded worker pool and bounded queue; saturation returns HTTP 503, completions return through ev_async, and handler generations fence stale results. A separate 5/5 Docker/netem artifact proves slow/fast concurrency, queue saturation, and stale-handler survival against the real state engine through a test-only delay proxy. Each verified connection now derives its bounded publisher identity from the peer certificate URI SAN. Per-identity pending limits return HTTP 429 and round-robin identity queues prevent one overloaded publisher's pending queue from monopolizing another publisher; a 5/5 Docker/netem gate covers two identities and an out-of-prefix fail-closed control. An optional per-identity active-worker limit additionally prevents one identity from occupying the entire worker pool. A matched 5/5 limit-1 versus limit-2 contrast proves an independent publisher completes while both noisy-publisher clients remain open only in the isolated phase; the default limit equals the worker count to preserve existing work-conserving behavior. An opt-in public-GnuTLS path now reloads the client CRL before verification of every new TLS connection. A 5/5 Docker/netem artifact changes the live CRL without restarting the server, proves a newly revoked client is rejected with CRYPTO_ERROR, proves acceptance resumes after restoring the valid CRL, and proves a malformed replacement fails closed. Active-session revocation now closes this gap for already-established connections too: each successful CRL reload (still only triggered by a new handshake) also scans every live connection's cached peer-certificate serial against the freshly reloaded revoked-serial set and force-closes any match with a QUIC CONNECTION_REFUSED transport error, rather than only ever consulting the reload for new connections. A 5/5 Docker/netem gate keeps one connection open, revokes that exact connection's own certificate, then makes one unrelated new connection and confirms the first is torn down as a side effect while the second succeeds normally (docker_ngtcp2_public_active_session_revocation_probe). This does not add periodic/proactive revocation checking independent of a new handshake arriving. An opt-in online client-CA rotation now piggybacks on the same handshake-triggered reload path as the client CRL above -- it already rebuilt its GnuTLS credentials from both the CA trust file and the CRL file on every handshake, so replacing the CA file's on-disk content rotates which CA is trusted without a server restart, as a side effect of a mechanism only previously tested for revocation. A 5/5 Docker/netem gate starts trusting CA-A, confirms a CA-B-signed client is rejected, swaps the CA file to CA-B, confirms a CA-B client is now accepted and a CA-A client is now rejected (a genuine rotation, not an addition), then restores CA-A and confirms it works again, all against the same live server process (docker_ngtcp2_public_online_client_ca_rotation_probe). Online server-certificate rotation is now also implemented, but needed a genuinely new hook rather than reuse of the client-CA one above: the server sends its own certificate to the client before the point in the handshake where that reload runs, so it cannot affect what gets presented. server-certificate-rotation.patch adds a second, independent reload in TLSServerSession::init() (once per new connection, before any handshake message is sent) that rebuilds credentials from FLEETQOX_GNUTLS_SERVER_CERT/_KEY plus the client CA/CRL this object must also still carry -- including re-registering client-certificate chain verification on the fresh object, since that is a per-credentials-object property that does not carry over from the original. Proving it exposed a real gap in the shared test harness itself: the vendored gtlsclient never verifies the server's certificate at all (no verification function is ever registered client-side), so accept/reject was not a valid signal for what the server presented. client-server-cert-verification.patch adds an opt-in --verify-server-cert flag to a separately built fleetqox-public-mtls-client binary (default gtlsclient behavior is completely unchanged for the ~185 other probes that depend on it) that actually checks the server's chain. A 5/5 Docker/netem gate starts trusting server-CA-A, confirms a verifying client is rejected by a CA-B-signed server certificate, swaps the certificate files to a CA-B-signed pair, confirms a CA-A-trusting client is now rejected and a CA-B-trusting client is now accepted, then restores the original certificate and confirms acceptance resumes, all against the same live server process (docker_ngtcp2_public_online_server_certificate_rotation_probe). Production operations, clustered public-edge state, weighted QoS traffic classes, and broad overload policy remain unclaimed

partial.events: new message/request/response callbacks are supported; QoS event object init/fini and callback setters are supported; offered/requested deadline missed events are produced by a timer after the first publish/receive or on the next publish/receive after a deadline gap; publication/subscription matched, reliability/durability/deadline/liveliness-incompatible QoS, and exact type-incompatible events are produced for local endpoints, with matched, reliability/durability/deadline-incompatible QoS, and exact type events also produced for UDP-learned remote graph endpoints; local liveliness incompatibility covers automatic/manual kind, slower offered lease, missing offered lease, both offered/requested events, and a compatible control across 5/5 Docker runs. Remote advertisement renewal is deduplicated and explicit remove or graph-lease expiry updates matched and finite-liveliness changed state; subscription message-lost events are produced for KEEP_LAST queue overwrite, best-effort source-sequence gaps after a configurable grace interval, and subscriber-targeted reliable writer-history, repair-budget, repair-attempt, or repair-admission exhaustion, with first-sample join baselining and late repair/reorder suppression. The reliable history-exhaustion path passes 20/20 two-container Docker/netem runs; a second artifact proves budget=0, max-attempt=1, and strict-admission rejection 5/5 each. Duplicate notices are merged into one sample/event and every process tears down cleanly. Local MANUAL_BY_TOPIC liveliness lost/changed events are produced for finite lease timeout and explicit reassert. AUTOMATIC finite-lease publishers are renewed by the middleware while alive; a 5/5 Docker control remains idle for six lease periods with no false lost callback or wait readiness. Remote MANUAL_BY_TOPIC publishers use an independent wire assertion sent by explicit assert and publish; a 5/5 two-container UDP/netem artifact proves idle expiry without unmatching, both reassert paths, publisher-side lost callback/wait/take, and independence from periodic graph renewal. A second 5/5 remote artifact proves independent state across two simultaneous publishers, alive/not-alive removal, exact aggregate liveliness counts, and remove/recreate churn of a third endpoint while expiry remains distinct from matching. A local 5/5 scale artifact proves exact aggregate transitions across 64 MANUAL_BY_TOPIC publishers, independent keepalive/expiry/reassert/removal halves, and 16 idle SYSTEM_DEFAULT publishers that remain alive for six finite lease periods. A two-container UDP/netem scale artifact repeats 5/5 with 64 remote MANUAL_BY_TOPIC publishers, exact half-expiry/reassert/all-expiry/removal and matched deltas, 96 expiries, 32 reassertions, and matching preserved through expiry. Default/non-expiring leases retain alive/remove lifecycle events without false timeout for SYSTEM_DEFAULT, AUTOMATIC, MANUAL_BY_TOPIC, BEST_AVAILABLE, and MANUAL_BY_NODE in a 5/5 artifact; only UNKNOWN endpoint inputs fail closed. MANUAL_BY_NODE (deprecated upstream in favor of MANUAL_BY_TOPIC, but still accepted from applications that have not migrated) shares one liveliness assertion across every MANUAL_BY_NODE publisher owned by the same node, matching DDS MANUAL_BY_PARTICIPANT semantics: a local 5/5 artifact proves a silent sibling publisher is kept alive by another publisher's asserts on the same node, that the shared lease still expires normally once every publisher on that node goes idle, and that sharing does not leak across a node boundary; a two-container UDP/netem 5/5 artifact proves the same sharing and expiry over the real wire, grouped by domain_id + node_name + node_namespace already carried in every graph advertisement. Unread statuses for all eleven non-invalid Jazzy event types become ready through rmw_wait and are consumed through rmw_take_event in a 5/5 aggregate matrix (35/35 components). Four repeated real UDP/netem source artifacts additionally cover callback/wait/take paths for all eleven event types over 35 executions. Remote liveliness-incompatible QoS is also proven over a real two-container UDP/netem wire: a dedicated 5/5 artifact exercises both AUTOMATIC-vs-MANUAL_BY_TOPIC kind mismatch and slow-vs-fast lease-duration mismatch, in both directions (a local publisher against a remote-learned subscription, and a local subscription against a remote-learned publisher), using the same incompatible_qos_policy_kind() code path already shared with local matching. Full DDS message-lost/resource-limit semantics and the full QoS/type compatibility matrix are not implemented, and are architecturally bounded rather than pending effort: rmw_qos_profile_t (upstream rmw/types.h) has no resource_limits fields, and rmw_qos_policy_kind_t (upstream rmw/qos_policy_kind.h) has no enum values for OWNERSHIP/PRESENTATION/PARTITION/DESTINATION_ORDER, so message-lost-by-resource-limit and non-deadline QoS event production cannot be closed without forking upstream rmw. Remote type-incompatible-event detection now uses each side's RIHS structural type hash (rosidl_type_hash_t, from get_type_hash_func) as the authoritative check when both a local and a remote-learned endpoint carry a valid one: a dedicated 5/5 two-container UDP/netem artifact proves a same-declared-type-name-but-different-structural-hash mismatch is detected in both directions (a mismatch plain type_name comparison could never see), alongside a matching-hash compatible control and a no-valid-hash fallback control that keeps the prior type_name-equality behavior intact for every hand-built probe type support elsewhere in this suite that has no get_type_hash_func. This closes the remote structural type-hash gap for event production; it does not change how the transport actually matches/routes messages (that remains type_name-based, a separate, larger redesign not attempted here)
partial.content_filters: subscription content-filter set/get stores and returns expression parameters, marks the subscription CFT-enabled, supports dynamic reconfigure and empty-expression disable, and enforces parameterized = != <> > >= < <= predicates plus SQL-like AND/OR/NOT precedence, parentheses, LIKE, BETWEEN, IN/NOT IN, IS NULL, and IS NOT NULL. Evaluation covers key-value text, std_msgs/String-style payloads, and direct ROSIDL introspection C/C++ reflection of nested scalar paths; C++ sequence fields additionally expose indexed paths such as data[1], length paths such as data._length, and nested sequence-message paths such as layout.dim[0].label. Typed reflection parses the bounded FleetRMW wire payload directly without constructing an application message and fails closed on malformed metadata or payload bounds. Missing fields retain SQL unknown through negation; malformed expressions and missing parameter references fail closed. WSTRING fields (ROSIDL introspection C/C++) are now reflected for filtering too: the wire-format UTF-16 code units are decoded, including surrogate pairs for code points outside the Basic Multilingual Plane, into UTF-8 text for the same predicate engine used for string fields; a dedicated probe proves round-trip fidelity through general serialize/deserialize (not just filtering) for a field mixing an accented BMP character with a surrogate-pair emoji, plus correct filter admit/drop against that reflected text (docker_wstring_content_filter_probe). Comparison predicates (=, !=, <>, <, <=, >, >=) also accept the DDS-SQL-standard reversed operand order (a parameter or quoted literal on the left, e.g. %0 = field_name or %1 < field_name), not just field-first comparisons, proven by a dedicated scenario plus a malformed-reversed-form negative control in docker_content_filter_sql_probe. The full DDS SQL expression dialect, arbitrary DDS SQL functions, and vendor-specific content-filter semantics remain not implemented
partial.security: rmw_init_options security-options lifecycle, enclave copy, context init copy, shutdown, fini, opt-in FleetQoX publish allow/deny rules, and a scoped SROS2-generated DDS permissions, governance, and local identity validation path are covered by repeated Docker probes and the stress/security campaign. FleetRMW verifies permissions.p7s and governance.p7s at runtime, validates local identity before rmw_init, and enforces permissions plus Governance access-control across topic/service/Action paths. The UDP AEAD v2 envelope uses AES-256-GCM with HKDF-SHA256 PSK session derivation/reuse/rotation, signed random salts, nonce replay tracking, SROS2 X.509 peer signatures, identity allowlists, CA-chain validation, and CRL revocation; valid paths and tamper, unauthorized-identity, untrusted-CA, revoked-certificate, and missing-key controls pass 5/5. A two-peer fragmented-sample gate proves that strict AEAD rejects unprotected repair and outer fragment wrappers before reassembly admission and keeps six authenticated incomplete samples within a four-assembly bound. A three-peer campaign independently recreates credentials/network/processes and passes 5/5; a CA-trusted unauthorized identity uses the same PSK, 481 data/graph inputs are denied by identity with a per-run minimum of 95, and reassembly/decryption state remains unchanged. The SROS2 identity CRL used to authenticate UDP AEAD peers is now reloaded live: udp_peer_auth_trust_store_ used to be built exactly once at process startup from FLEETQOX_RMW_SROS2_IDENTITY_CRL_FILE, so a certificate revoked after a long-running node started stayed trusted until restart. Every verification now checks the CRL file's mtime and rebuilds the trust store (CA plus fresh CRL) when it changed, verified by a probe that revokes a still-running process's own certificate mid-run and confirms its next self-authenticated message is rejected without a restart (docker_udp_peer_auth_crl_reload_probe); a failed reload keeps the last good store rather than failing closed, since this store also carries the process's own CA trust anchor and no fresher CRL was validated to justify discarding a still-good one over a transient read error. This is not DDS-Security interoperability or forward-secret asymmetric key exchange, and long-duration multi-attacker plus production PKI/transport hardening remain unimplemented
partial.benchmark_reporting: unified report aggregator normalizes existing JSON summary artifacts and capability claim boundaries without rerunning benchmarks, including the 8/16/32-robot three-seed split-scope and same-hop DDS/Cyclone/Zenoh comparisons, ns-3 artifacts, the OMNeT++ 6.4/INET 4.7 Docker runtime and matched routed-P2P bounded-parity matrix, and Docker stress/security campaign artifacts. The same-hop harness uses a common rclcpp generic subscription/publisher relay that forwards opaque serialized std_msgs/String payloads without application deserialization and a bounded wait-for-all-acked publisher horizon. After the reception-baseline cumulative-ACK fixes, the v4 common-middle artifact replaces all nine historical raw-router FleetRMW rows with direct-peer RMW terminate/republish rows while preserving the 27 generic-relay Fast DDS, Cyclone DDS, and Zenoh rows. The matrix passes 36/36, relays 6720/6720 payloads, and completes all 36 ACK horizons. Nine rows carry the explicit termination/republish field and 27 earlier-schema rows satisfy a strict generic-subscription/generic-publisher relay contract. Delivery/reliability, matched serialized-payload state, common middle application processing, and scoped latency-distribution comparison are allowed. Byte-identical cross-RMW serialization, broad latency superiority, architectural superiority, and production superiority remain disallowed because the campaign has only three repetitions per cell and no broad sensitivity campaign
partial.benchmark_resume_provenance: same-hop resume validates image, profile, netem loss scale, sample count, publish interval, generic relay mode/scope, required netem, and publisher reliability horizon before reusing a row. An exact v4-to-v5 control reuses 36/36 rows and preserves 6720/6720 relay payloads. A Docker negative control supplies the roaming artifact to a Wi-Fi run; both keyed candidates are rejected as configuration mismatches, FleetRMW and Cyclone DDS execute again, and both pass with 160/160 relay payloads
partial.benchmark_profile_sensitivity: the common-middle full-factorial profile-by-scale campaign covers 8,16,32 robots; Wi-Fi, WAN, and roaming; seeds 7,13,29; and FleetRMW, Fast DDS, Cyclone DDS, and Zenoh. Wi-Fi and WAN contribute 72 fresh Docker/netem rows; roaming reuses 36 configuration-matched v4 rows. All 108/108 rows pass and relay 20160/20160 payloads. Profile/scale-scoped delivery/reliability and latency-distribution comparison are allowed; broad cross-RMW, latency, architectural, and production superiority remain disallowed because there are only three repetitions per cell and one sample/resource schedule
partial.benchmark_payload_sensitivity: the matched common-middle payload campaign fixes roaming, 16 robots, five samples per topic, a 50 ms batch interval, seeds 7,13,29, and exact 256/4096/32768-byte UTF-8 payloads for all four RMWs. Every one of the 36 requested cells is measured with exact min/max byte evidence; 18/36 satisfy the complete delivery/ACK/process contract and the relay forwards 3855/5760 payloads. At 256 bytes all systems pass 3/3; at 4096 bytes Fast DDS and Cyclone DDS pass 3/3 while FleetRMW and Zenoh pass 0/3; at 32768 bytes all systems pass 0/3 under the fixed 5 Mbit/s, 7% loss offered-load schedule. FleetRMW's own 9 of these 36 cells (3 seeds x 3 payload sizes) have since been rerun after the same ENOBUFS fix: 256 bytes remains 960/960 (6/6 passing), 4096 bytes rises from 0/3 to a fully passing 960/960 (6/6), and 32768 bytes rises from 0/3 to 943/960 with one fully passing cell. The other three systems' 27 cells do not exercise FleetRMW code and were not rerun, so the original 36-cell/18-passing aggregate is not superseded, only FleetRMW's own contribution to it. The same offered-load-versus-capacity pattern applies here: at 50 ms intervals, 256/4096/32768-byte payloads demand 1.311/20.972/167.772 Mbit/s against the profile's 5 Mbit/s link (0.3x/4.2x/33.6x of capacity) -- 256 bytes is under capacity and passes outright, while 32768 bytes is 33.6x oversubscribed and cannot reach 100% by repair-protocol tuning alone. Delivery/reliability payload sensitivity is comparable, but payload-scoped latency distribution, broad superiority, and production claims remain disallowed because the frontier includes all-failed cells, only three repetitions, and no offered-load or host-resource sweep
partial.benchmark_offered_load_sensitivity: the matched common-middle offered-load campaign fixes roaming, 16 robots, five samples per topic, exact 32768-byte UTF-8 payloads, seeds 7,13,29, and all four RMWs while changing only the batch interval across 50/500/2000 ms. These intervals correspond to source-publisher application-payload rates of 167.772/16.777/4.194 Mbit/s before ROS/wire overhead and excluding the relay hop. All 36/36 cells are measured with exact schedule and byte evidence, but 0/36 satisfy the full delivery/ACK/process contract and relay delivery is 1149/5760; no fully successful interval is observed. Delivery/reliability offered-load sensitivity is comparable, but latency, sustainable-rate, superiority, and production claims remain disallowed. The lack of recovery even below the nominal 5 Mbit/s source link rate shows that burst shape, IP/transport fragmentation, packet loss, repair granularity, and protocol overhead must be studied rather than attributing the frontier to average offered load alone. FleetRMW's own 9 of these 36 cells (3 seeds x 3 intervals) have since been rerun after root-causing an uncaught ENOBUFS send failure that was crashing the publisher under this same 16-robot/32 KB link pressure (see loss_resilient_large_sample_fragment_repair): delivery rises to 891/960 at 50 ms, 944/960 at 500 ms, and a fully passing 960/960 at 2000 ms -- the first fully successful cell observed anywhere in this campaign. The other three systems' 27 cells do not exercise FleetRMW code and were not rerun, so the original 36-cell/1149-of-5760 aggregate is not superseded, only FleetRMW's own contribution to it. The pattern across intervals is explained by offered load versus the profile's actual 5 Mbit/s link rate, not by residual software defects: 50 ms/500 ms demand 167.772/16.777 Mbit/s (33.6x/3.4x oversubscribed), while 2000 ms demands only 4.194 Mbit/s (0.8x, i.e. under capacity) -- the one interval that reaches 100%. No protocol can deliver 33.6x more data than a link's capacity without loss or unbounded queuing; closing the oversubscribed cells would require senders that adapt their own rate to observed link conditions (see the unclaimed adaptive capacity control item below), not further repair-protocol tuning
partial.serialization_size: exact recursive size for statically bounded introspection C/C++ messages; artificial bounds for unbounded fields are unsupported
partial.allocations: publisher/subscription allocation init/fini allocate a type-support-bound, mutex-protected payload scratch buffer; typed and serialized publish/take reuse its capacity. A 5/5 Docker artifact performs eight publish/take pairs per process with exact use counts, stable 65536-byte capacity, zero payload-scratch growths, and rejection of an uninitialized allocation. Frame encoding now also reuses a persistent per-publisher buffer (FleetQoxPublisherData::frame_base64_scratch) for the serialized payload's base64 text across repeated publishes, instead of allocating a fresh string on every single publish call; a dedicated 5/5 Docker artifact (docker_deep_preallocation_probe) publishes eight same-size payloads per process and proves the buffer's capacity grows once on the first publish then stays exactly stable for the remaining seven, rebuilt clean under ASan/UBSan with zero diagnostics. This is a genuine, bounded reduction, not a closure of the full claim: the JSON frame body itself is still built through a fresh std::ostringstream per publish (its floating-point field formatting is deliberately left untouched -- rewriting it risks silently changing on-wire number formatting depended on by roughly 187 other probes), the reliability retransmit ledger still allocates a new entry (encoded frame copy plus a subscriber-ID set) per in-flight reliable message by design since it is an unbounded, QoS-depth-driven store-and-forward buffer, and application-message deserialization is unchanged. Full deep/all-hot-path preallocation would require a binary (non-JSON) wire format and a pool allocator for the retransmit ledger, and remains unclaimed
partial.loaned_messages: middleware-owned publisher/subscription loan lifecycle for introspection C/C++; subscription take currently deserializes into the loan and is not zero-copy. The loan buffer itself is now pooled per publisher/subscription (g_loan_pool) instead of allocating a fresh block on every borrow_loan() call: release_loan() runs the type's fini_function to release any heap-owned sub-fields (std::string/vector internal buffers) then returns the raw block to a capped per-owner pool (8 buffers) instead of deallocating it, and borrow_loan() checks that pool before falling back to a fresh allocation. A dedicated 5/5 Docker artifact (docker_deep_preallocation_loaned_message_probe) proves exactly one fresh allocation occurs for a subscription's entire lifetime of repeated take/return cycles, with every other cycle reusing the pool, rebuilt clean under ASan/UBSan with zero diagnostics. This does not close the zero-copy claim: it removes the allocation, not the deserialization -- the JSON+base64 wire format and variable-length introspection fields (std::string/vector) mean the loaned buffer can never alias the received network bytes directly, so the transcode from wire text to typed struct is unavoidable without a binary wire format matching the in-memory layout
